Each time there is a close election people whinge about the electoral college, call it "outdated," and generally make idiots of themselves. The electoral college is not some relic from a horse-and-buggy era, it's a sophisticated and important tool for managing the will of the people in the United States.

The purpose of the electoral college is to prevent any one region from overloading the total vote to get their candidate selected over the will of majorities in other parts of the country.

The United States is a federation and from the beginning has consisted of agrarian, rural, urban, religious, and other types of regions. Balancing these differences has always been a critical component of making the US government function in a representative manner. By assigning a proportional total of electoral votes to each state you eliminate the ability of any particular outlier to overly influence the election.

This year what you have is a very strong vote for one candidate in one particular state - California. California is a large state and for whatever reason has STRONGLY gone in favor of the losing candidate. Over this large of a population it's fair to say that there is some form of distortion occurring in that one region. If that distortion is allowed to overtake the rest of the country's will then your republic is a sham and people will not support it. This could just as easily have been a VERY strong vote in the South over-ruling the Northeast, Midwest, and Western states. The electoral college balances this "excess support" phenomenon very fairly.

A comparable example to consider is the state of Virginia. The bulk of Virginia votes one way, but a tiny slice of the northern end of the state, owing to its status as an suburb of the federal capital across the state line, bulks up on the vote, favoring one candidate heavily and thus overrides the will of the rest of the state. On a Federal level this would be a catastrophe.

So that's what the electoral college is for. It's the REAL election. The popular vote doesn't mean anything because people with brains understand how it works and it does suppress turnout and enthusiasm and can also allow people to strategically alter their votes in states with a strong likelihood of choosing a "safe" candidate. If the popular vote were what determined the election then campaigns would be entirely different and VOTERS would be entirely different. I don't doubt that if you held this same contest next week using a popular vote model that Trump would win again - this time he'd get very high turnouts in areas that went extremely for Trump and it would properly balance California.

Ultimately, the lesson here is that the electoral college protects us from fanaticism and that something is clearly wrong with people in California who don't seem to understand how it functions.
